ECE 6612

SSO and passkeys

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows a federated login token and a passkey proof arriving at their intended verifiers.

Single Sign-On (SSO) lets several services rely on one identity provider (IdP) to authenticate users. The destination is a service provider (SP), also called a relying party in identity systems. The browser participates in redirects or message delivery. In the signed-token model, the IdP authenticates the user, creates protected identity claims, and the SP verifies that evidence before creating its own session.

A signature check requires a key belonging to a trusted issuer. The SP also checks the intended audience, validity times and binding to the current login request, including the protocol’s nonce or other request-correlation values. A signed claim for one service has an intended recipient; that recipient check keeps it from becoming a general login pass. The exact exchanges depend on the federation protocol. SAML means Security Assertion Markup Language; OpenID Connect supplies authentication on top of the OAuth 2.0 authorization framework.

A common IdP can centralize strong authentication and reduce repeated password entry and reuse. It also becomes a shared availability, privacy and signing-key dependency. Several services may fail together during an IdP outage, and a compromised trusted signing key can undermine the evidence those services accept. Each SP still decides what an authenticated account may do.

A passkey is a public-key credential associated with a relying party. During registration, an authenticator creates or protects a key pair and the service records the credential’s public key with the account. The private key remains under the protection of the authenticator or passkey provider. A local PIN or biometric check can authorize its use. A synced passkey may be securely copied through its provider’s system, making that provider’s account and recovery protections part of the trust model.

During authentication the service supplies a fresh challenge. The authenticator signs an assertion that binds the response to the relying party and the browser exchange. The service verifies the signature with the stored public key and checks the expected challenge, relying-party identifier, origin and required user-presence or user-verification flags. The browser/authenticator protocol restricts credential use to the relying party’s scope, giving phishing resistance when the complete validation succeeds.

WebAuthn means Web Authentication and defines the browser interface. FIDO2 combines WebAuthn with authenticator protocols. A passkey’s local unlock value authorizes key use on the device; the service verifies the resulting public-key proof. Enrollment, account linking, lost-device recovery and alternate login methods can all lead to the same account, so their trust checks belong in a complete authentication design.

Example

An IdP signs a token with audience “library” during a library login. Payroll receives a copied token with a valid signature. Its audience check rejects the token for payroll. In a passkey login, replaying yesterday’s assertion fails the fresh challenge check even when that old signature still verifies over yesterday’s assertion.

Sources and scope
  • C17 Web Authentication: SSO trust roles and passkey enrollment/login.
  • OpenID Connect Core: ID token validation and nonce binding.
  • W3C Web Authentication: registration and authentication verification.

Practice

1. A service verifies an IdP token’s signature but accepts any audience and request nonce. Which checks should it complete, and what does each establish?

Identify issuer, destination, time and current login exchange.

It must use the trusted issuer’s key and validate the expected issuer, its own audience, permitted validity period and the federation protocol’s current-request binding such as the expected nonce. These establish who issued the claims, which service they target, when they apply and which login they answer. Authorization follows after authentication.

2. A service stores a passkey public key. What additional values must a successful login assertion be checked against, and why does a fresh challenge matter?

Follow the registration binding and this login’s browser exchange.

The service checks the signature with the registered key, the expected challenge, relying-party identifier, allowed origin, and required presence/verification flags under WebAuthn’s rules. The fresh challenge binds the proof to this authentication attempt and prevents an old assertion from serving as a new proof.
